Exercise #1 — Distributions, Simulation, and the Log-Likelihood

PLSC 606J, Fall 2026

Author
Affiliation

Dave Clark

Binghamton University

Published

August 19, 2026

On this page

  • Part I — Distributions and links
  • Part II — Simulation and the log-likelihood
  • Part III — Estimation and Interpretation
    • Notes

Please answer the following questions. All answers should be coded in R and submitted as a rendered PDF built in Quarto (or R Markdown) or LaTeX. Please turn in both your source (.qmd/.R) and the rendered document on Brightspace, so I can run exactly what you ran. Everything should be instantly replicable — running your code should reproduce every figure, table, and number.

For this assignment, the only R libraries you need (should use) are

  • tidyverse for data management and plotting
  • patchwork for the side-by-side panels in question #1
  • modelsummary, gt, kableExtra, or comparable for professional tables

This assignment is aimed at developing coding skills and habits, an understanding of probability distributions and their relationship to data, and some basic data management. It also reviews the logit and probit and prediction methods.

About the figures. Questions 1–4 each show you a figure and ask you to replicate it. I mean replicate: same curves, same axes, same labeling, same look. Part of what you’re learning this term is how to produce a figure someone else would be willing to publish, and the fastest way to learn that is to reproduce one and notice every decision that went into it — the palette, the linetypes, the axis labels, where the legend sits, what the title claims. The prediction plots you build in question 10 should meet the same standard.

Work with each other — that’s essential — but the work you turn in must be your own.

On AI tools. Per the course policy: if you get stuck coding, you may use a bot to get unstuck, but you must cite and annotate it (what you asked, why, and which lines are the bot’s), and expect to explain your work. Don’t start with a bot — the point of the exercise is what you come to understand by writing the code.

Part I — Distributions and links

For this section, please write out all PDF/CDF equations — that is, do not use built-in R functions (plogis, dlogis, pcauchy, dnorm and so on) except for pnorm (so you don’t have to write the integral). Write the equations yourself.

1. Please replicate this figure. What do the PDFs describe? What do the CDFs describe?

2. Please replicate this figure — it overlays the CDFs of

  • the logistic
  • the complementary log-log (cloglog)
  • the log-log

Comment on the differences among the three.

3. Please replicate this figure — it overlays the logistic CDF with intercepts of \(-1\), \(0\), and \(+1\). Please describe what happens as the intercept changes. Then compare these intercept shifts to intercept shifts in the linear model: how are the two similar, and how are they different?

4. Please replicate this figure — it overlays the skewed logit (scobit) CDF at shape parameters \(\alpha = 1\), \(\alpha = 2\), and \(\alpha = 0.5\). Please describe what happens as the shape parameter changes. How are these curves similar to, and different from, the logistic CDF in question 3?

Part II — Simulation and the log-likelihood

5. Please write code that simulates data for a binary \(y\) variable from the equation \(x\beta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2\), with \(\beta_0 = -1\), \(\beta_1 = 0.5\), and \(\beta_2 = -0.5\), with a logit link. Let \(x_1\) be continuous and \(x_2\) be binary. The output should be a data frame of 1,000 observations containing a binary \(y\), a constant, and the two \(x\) variables.

6. Please write (in proper math notation, not code) the likelihood and log-likelihood functions for a binary \(y\) variable using the logit as the link function. Describe the parts of the log-likelihood and what each is doing.

7. Please write the log-likelihood function from above in R code, as a function. It should take as arguments a vector of parameters, a matrix of \(X\) variables, and a \(y\) variable, and return a single number (the log-likelihood). Using the data from question #5 for \(X\) and \(y\), evaluate the log-likelihood at:

  • the true \(\beta\)’s from question #5
  • the \(\beta\)’s from a glm logit of the data and equation from question #5
  • \(\beta\) values of 0, 0, 0
  • \(\beta\) values of 1, -.5, .5

Present the log-likelihoods in a professional table and comment.

Part III — Estimation and Interpretation

Here’s a link to a dataset called ces.csv. It contains individual-level data from the Cooperative Election Study for the 2020 election, via the “American Voter Bot” on Twitter. Variable descriptions are in the data; more information is in the notes below. GitHub won’t preview a file this size, so click Download raw file, and put it in a data/ folder inside your project so here::here("data", "ces.csv") finds it.

You’ll need to look carefully at the variables and recode/clean as necessary prior to estimation — please include all of that code so it replicates.

8. Please estimate logit and probit models predicting vote choice as a function of whatever variables you think are relevant. Present a professional table of the estimates in side-by-side columns and discuss. Explain your thinking about the models — why did you include these variables, and what did you expect?

9. Please compute odds ratios for the variables of interest in the logit model, and discuss them. What do they tell you?

10. Please generate predicted probabilities and intervals from both models and present professional plots — separately, one plot for each model. For the logit, please use average effects; for the probit, please use at-mean effects. For both, the \(x\) axis should be a continuous variable, and each plot should show two lines, one for each value of a binary variable of interest. Please write the code for these yourself — that is, don’t call a package that produces the predictions or marginal effects for you.

Write a couple of sentences describing/interpreting your figures (as you would in a journal article).

Notes

The CES project site is https://cces.gov.harvard.edu. Here’s an article about the “American Voter Bot” project: https://www.nytimes.com/2020/01/20/opinion/twitter-democratic-debate.html
